**CPU (Central Processing Unit)**  
- **Purpose:** General‑purpose processor designed to handle a wide variety of tasks.  
- **Architecture:** Few cores (typically 2–32) but each core is very powerful, with deep pipelines, large caches, and sophisticated branch prediction.  
- **Execution model:** Executes complex, branching instructions one at a time (or a few at a time). Good at serial workloads.  
- **Typical use cases:** Operating systems, application logic, database queries, web servers, gaming logic, etc.  
- **Performance metric:** Measured in FLOPS per core, but more importantly in instructions per cycle (IPC) and clock speed.  

**GPU (Graphics Processing Unit)**  
- **Purpose:** Originally built to accelerate rendering of images and video. Now used for massively parallel workloads (machine learning, scientific simulation, cryptocurrency mining, etc.).  
- **Architecture:** Hundreds to thousands of lightweight cores arranged in SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) groups. Each core is simpler, with smaller caches and less sophisticated control logic.  
- **Execution model:** Executes the same instruction on many data elements simultaneously. Excellent for data‑parallel tasks where the same operation is repeated over large arrays.  
- **Typical use cases:** Rendering graphics, deep‑learning inference/training, high‑performance computing (HPC), video encoding/decoding, etc.  
- **Performance metric:** Measured in FLOPS per second; GPUs can deliver tens of teraflops for floating‑point operations.  

**Key Differences Summarized**

| Feature | CPU | GPU |
|---------|-----|-----|
| Core count | Few, powerful | Many, lightweight |
| Instruction complexity | High, branching | Simple, SIMD |
| Workload type | Serial/branching | Parallel, data‑parallel |
| Memory hierarchy | Large L1/L2/L3 caches | Smaller caches, high memory bandwidth |
| Typical clock speed | Higher | Lower |
| Energy efficiency | Better for single‑thread tasks | Better for throughput tasks |

In short, a CPU is a versatile “brain” for general tasks, while a GPU is a specialized “worker” that excels when you need to perform the same operation on thousands or millions of data points simultaneously.
